sn5.2:1.2: For Pasenadi’s wife of the same name, see [mn90:3.1]() and note.
sn5.2:2.3: “Two-inch wisdom” (_dvaṅgulapaññā_), literally “two finger(-breadth’s) wisdom, is explained by the commentary as limited wisdom; or because women hold thread between two fingers. The subcommentary and the commentary to the Therīgāthā say it is because women test whether rice is cooked by pressing a grain between two fingers. Normally, _aṅgula_ with a number is a unit of length equal to the width of the middle finger, which is often a “small amount”. For example, the time past noon is measured when the sun’s shadow moves two inches ([pli-tv-kd22:1.10.16]()), which is the same distance the shadow moves each month (Arthaśāstra 2.20.42). Thus the first commentarial explanation is the most plausible, “two inch wisdom” means “limited wisdom”. The late literary text Bṛhatkathāślokasaṁgraha employs the same idiom, by a woman to dismiss women’s wit (22.35)—as so often, a woman makes the best misogynist—or by a man who muses that perhaps man like him are the real fools since they allow women to entice them (22.302–3).
sn5.2:2.4: It is Māra, not the Buddha, who doubts women’s capacity.
sn5.2:5.1: Somā’s verses at [thig3.8]() lack this verse.
sn5.2:5.3: Reading asmīti with other translators. But surely the Upanishadic echoes should be preserved here; it gets lost if we abbreviate “I’m”. She’s not just dismissing other conceptions of ultimate gender identity, but even the supposed post-gender Upanishadic self.
